title: Ban on data centers (initiated ordinance)
target_project: Project Milo (near Deer Creek Golf Course)
summary: Citizen-initiated ordinance prohibiting the construction of any data center within city limits, including converting existing buildings. No megawatt threshold: the only outright ban among Ohio's November measures. Council had already adopted a 12-month moratorium.
ballot_text: Proposed ordinance to approve or reject a ban on data centers within the City limits (Trumbull County Board of Elections description; full ballot language not yet retrieved).
notes: Issue number not yet confirmed; check Trumbull BOE sample ballot.

title: Charter amendment banning data centers over 7.5 MW
target_project: Thor Equities proposal south of Rittal
proponents: Conserve Ohio / Nicole Nawman petition (400+ signatures)
summary: Adds Section 8.07 to Article VIII of the city charter prohibiting construction of data centers in the city, with an exemption for small privately owned facilities serving a single organization with peak demand under 7.5 MW. Council rescinded its data-center zoning allowance in June and adopted a 12-month moratorium; Thor Equities sued in federal court. A recall of the mayor is on the same ballot.
ballot_text: Shall Article VIII of the Charter of the City of Urbana be amended to add Section 8.07, to read as follows? (Section 8.07: the construction of a data center is prohibited, exempting a wholly owned facility serving a single organization with peak electrical demand below 7.5 megawatts; summary of the section text per the Urbana Daily Citizen)

title: Charter amendment banning data centers over 25 MW
target_project: Amazon Data Services campus (~$2B) in the city technology park
summary: Adds Article XI, Section 11.05 to the city charter prohibiting construction of data centers with aggregate monthly demand or peak electrical load over 25 MW. Self-executing. Council enacted a moratorium through Jan 31, 2027 while the vote is pending.
ballot_text: Shall Article XI, Section 11.05 of the Charter of the City of Sunbury be adopted? (Section 11.05, Prohibition of Construction of a Data Center: defines a data center as one or more facilities on a parcel or aggregated adjacent parcels used primarily or exclusively for data processing or storage with an aggregate monthly demand or peak load over 25 megawatts; self-executing; majority vote required.)
notes: Delaware County Issue 9 is a different Sunbury charter amendment (council seats); confirm this measure's issue number.

title: Charter amendment banning data centers over 25 MW
target_project: No formal proposal (M2 Development feasibility study at Conneaut East Industrial Park)
opponents: City Manager Nick Sanford warned of judicial review
summary: Adds Article XVI, Conservation of Natural Resources, to the city charter, prohibiting data centers with aggregate monthly demand or peak load over 25 MW (318 valid signatures). Council declined to adopt a moratorium; the petition went forward anyway.
ballot_text: Charter amendment prohibiting the construction of data centers with aggregate monthly demand or peak load greater than 25 megawatts (summary; verbatim text not yet retrieved).

title: Charter amendment banning data centers over 25 MW
summary: Adds Section 1.12 to the city charter prohibiting construction of data centers with a monthly or peak load greater than 25 MW. First petition-driven charter amendment since the 1983 charter; council also adopted a six-month moratorium.
ballot_text: Charter amendment adding Section 1.12 to Article I: the construction of a data center is hereby prohibited, with a data center defined at 25 megawatts or more (WTOL voter guide lists it as City of Defiance, proposed charter amendment: Prohibition of a data center; verbatim text not yet retrieved).

title: Charter amendment banning data centers over 25 MW
target_project: Proposed ~600-acre Amazon campus (Madison/St. Clair townships); existing AWS site unaffected
summary: Adds Article IX, Section 9.06 to the charter: data center construction is prohibited where aggregate monthly demand or peak load exceeds 25 MW from any energy source or combination; self-executing. Council refused to certify the petition until the Ohio Supreme Court ordered it onto the ballot (State ex rel. Blankenship v. Trenton City Council, 2026-Ohio-3406). Council has teed up a property-tax holiday contingent on the measure failing, and litigation is expected if it passes.
ballot_text: Shall the Charter of the City of Trenton be amended by adding Article IX, Section 9.06, providing that (A) data center construction is prohibited, defining a data center as a facility with an aggregate monthly demand or peak load greater than twenty-five megawatts, from any energy source or combination, and (D) that the section is self-executing? (partial text per WVXU and the Butler County Board of Elections)
notes: Ohio Supreme Court ordered the measure onto the ballot Sept 1, 2026.

title: Community Consent Amendment (voter approval for large developments)
target_project: ~300-acre data center proposal (Beatty/Rensch Rd)
summary: Creates a mandatory public referendum for any development of 50 or more acres, more than 20 MW peak demand, or more than 500,000 gallons of water per day, with the developer paying election costs. Not a ban, but it would subject the proposed data center to a citywide vote. City moratorium runs through June 2027.
ballot_text: Community Consent Amendment: creates a public referendum process for large developments (Franklin County Board of Elections certified description; full text at the county link).

title: Charter amendment banning data centers over 25 MW
target_project: Aligned Data Centers 200 MW, three-building site plan (rejected by council 7-0)
proponents: Citizen petition (500+ signatures, Conserve Ohio language)
summary: Adds Section 11.09 to the charter prohibiting construction of a data center within city limits, using the 25 MW monthly-demand definition. One of four Pataskala charter amendments on the ballot. Aligned is seeking judicial review of the council's rejection.
ballot_text: Charter amendment adding Section 11.09 to prohibit the construction of a data center within the City limits, defined by a 25 megawatt monthly demand (Licking County Board of Elections issues list; verbatim text not yet retrieved).
notes: The Licking County BOE summary shows no megawatt threshold; news reports describe the 25 MW definition. One of four Pataskala charter amendments plus a library levy on the same ballot.

title: Charter amendment prohibiting data centers (Section 10.12)
target_project: None proposed (largely symbolic)
summary: Adds Section 10.12 (Prohibition of a Data Center) to the village charter with the 25 MW definition. No project is proposed in Granville.
ballot_text: Village of Granville charter amendment adding Section 10.12, Prohibition of a Data Center (Licking County Board of Elections issues list; verbatim text not yet retrieved).
notes: Some roundups describe it as an outright ban; confirm threshold in the certified text.

title: Charter amendment capping data centers at 25 MW
target_project: Proposed data center on farmland in Oregon
summary: Writes a 25 MW cap into the city charter using the Conserve Ohio template. Organizers frame it as steering development to brownfield and industrial sites.
ballot_text: Charter amendment prohibiting data centers with aggregate monthly demand or peak load over 25 megawatts (summary; verbatim text not yet retrieved).
notes: Council accepted the BOE certification Aug 19. Lucas County reports on the SOS-hosted ENR platform (Nov 2025 was instance 21); Toledo's own charter amendment is Issue 17 on Lucas ballots, so Oregon's issue number differs.

title: Charter amendment banning data centers over 25 MW
target_project: ~150-acre, ~150 MW self-powered facility proposed north of town
summary: Charter amendment prohibiting data center construction using the 25 MW definition. Reported by Ohio Capital Journal and Ballotpedia; the weakest-confirmed Ohio entry, so verify with the Wyandot County Board of Elections.
ballot_text: Charter amendment prohibiting the construction of data centers (summary; verbatim text not yet retrieved).
notes: Still confirmed only via secondary sources (Ohio Capital Journal, Newsweek, Conserve Ohio). Verify with the Wyandot County BOE, (419) 294-1226, or its ballots page.

title: Advisory question on allowing data center development
target_project: Decimal Digital AI data center pitch
summary: Non-binding question asking whether village officials should allow data center development within village limits. The village adopted a 12-month moratorium in February and is still owed about $1.3M from a 2024 crypto-mining operation.
ballot_text: Advisory question: should village officials allow data center development within the village limits? (summary; verbatim text not yet retrieved)
notes: A YES vote favors allowing data centers.

title: Adopt township zoning to regulate a data center at the Stuart plant site
target_project: Data center at the former J.M. Stuart power plant site (federal permit issued)
summary: Township zoning adoption under ORC Chapter 519, which requires voter approval. Adopting zoning gives the township authority over the proposed data center at the former Stuart power plant; trustees passed a one-year voluntary moratorium in March.
ballot_text: Shall the zoning resolution and plan for Sprigg Township be adopted? (standard ORC 519 form; exact wording not yet retrieved)

title: Adopt township zoning to regulate a data center at the Killen plant site
target_project: Data center at the former Killen power plant site
summary: Township zoning adoption under ORC Chapter 519 covering the former Killen power plant site; trustees created a zoning commission in March.
ballot_text: Shall the zoning resolution and plan for Monroe Township be adopted? (standard ORC 519 form; exact wording not yet retrieved)

title: Referendum on Resolution 06-2026 (EdgeConneX development agreement)
target_project: EdgeConneX: two data centers and a gas plant on ~195 acres
proponents: Teays Valley Community Alliance (petition, 669 valid signatures)
summary: Referendum on the council's April resolution approving a development and supply agreement term summary with EdgeConneX. The Ohio Supreme Court ordered the petition certified (State ex rel. McNamara-Smith v. Grube, 2026-Ohio-3035). A YES vote upholds the agreement; a NO vote rejects it (though it does not by itself stop construction). EdgeConneX paid the village $3.5M in October.
ballot_text: Referendum on Resolution (By Petition): Shall the resolution enacting approval of a development and supply agreement term summary with EdgeConneX (Resolution 06-2026) be approved? YES = FOR the resolution; NO = AGAINST (per the Circleville Herald's report on the Pickaway County ballot proofs).
notes: A YES vote is the pro-data-center side. Council introduced Resolution 16-2026 in September to repeal the agreement, which under R.C. 731.34 could pull the question; October coverage still treats the vote as proceeding. Confirm with the Pickaway County BOE.

title: Rezoning referendum: 119.4 acres on SR 730 (Ordinance O-26-04)
target_project: Ardent Companies / TAC Data Centers parcels (deal reportedly terminated); separate from the AWS campus
proponents: Clinton County Residents for Responsible Development (1,529 signatures)
summary: One of four referendums on February council ordinances rezoning a combined ~546 acres between S US-68 and SR-730 from rural residential to light industrial for data center development. A YES vote approves the rezoning ordinance; a NO vote overturns it. The zoning is stayed pending the vote.
ballot_text: Referendum (By Petition) on Ordinance O-26-04, adopted Feb 19, 2026, rezoning 119.373 acres on SR 730 from rural residential to light industrial. YES = approve the ordinance; NO = reject it.
notes: Four separate ballot questions on parcels formerly tied to the Ardent Companies project (agreement terminated this summer). Separate petitions against the Sept 3 Amazon-related ordinances are NOT on Nov 3. Map dots are offset slightly so all four are visible.

ballot_text: Referendum (By Petition) on Ordinance O-26-06 rezoning 191.12 acres on McGuinn Road from rural residential to light industrial. YES = approve the ordinance; NO = reject it.

title: Ban on high-impact data centers in all zoning districts
target_project: Proposed data center bid (~$3M, funding source contested in court)
opponents: Regional Development Association of East Central Kansas; city staff
summary: Citizen-initiated ordinance (K.S.A. 12-3013) prohibiting the construction, installation, operation and maintenance of High Impact Data Centers in every zoning district. A High Impact Data Center is one with peak electrical load over 10 MW or daily water draw over 100,000 gallons, including server farms, colocation, AI training and crypto mining. A district court ordered the question onto the ballot; the city's declaratory-judgment case on whether the subject is a proper initiative is still pending, so if approved the ordinance takes effect only after a ruling. Companion Question #3 would ban large battery storage.
ballot_text: Explanatory Statement: This ordinance would prohibit the construction, installation, operation, and maintenance of High Impact Data Centers within the City of Emporia, Kansas. A "High Impact Data Center" is defined as a facility whose primary purpose is the housing, operation, and maintenance of computer servers and related infrastructure that requires a peak electrical load exceeding ten (10) megawatts or a daily water draw exceeding one hundred thousand (100,000) gallons. This term includes server farms, colocation facilities, AI training facilities, cryptocurrency mining operations, and similar high-density computing facilities. The prohibition would apply to all zoning districts within the City. [...] Shall the following ordinance be adopted? An Ordinance of the City of Emporia, Kansas prohibiting the installation and operation of High Impact Data Centers to protect the health, safety and welfare of the residents of Emporia, Kansas. (Verbatim fragments from the city ballot-information page; the ordinance's operative sections as printed were not retrieved.)
notes: Polls close 7 pm Central. Local Question No. 2; Question No. 3 is the companion battery-storage ban. A YES vote adopts the ordinance. The Emporia Gazette reports the petition text cites a nonexistent code article; the city's judicial-review case on whether the subject is a proper initiative is pending, so if approved the ordinance cannot take effect until that is resolved.

title: Ten-year ban on high-impact data centers and large battery storage
target_project: Possible data center project discussed in April 2026
opponents: City of El Dorado (lost court challenge)
summary: Citizen-initiated ordinance prohibiting High Impact Data Centers and Tier 2 and Tier 3 battery energy storage systems. Under K.S.A. 12-3013, if adopted by voters it cannot be amended or repealed by the commission for ten years without voter approval. The Butler County District Court ruled the petition a proper legislative subject; the commission placed it on the ballot 5-0 on Aug 25.
ballot_text: Shall the following ordinance be adopted? [ordinance title] prohibiting the installation and operation of High Impact Data Centers and Tier 2 and Tier 3 Battery Energy Storage Systems. Per the city, the question as printed carries the ordinance title, the definitions (a high impact data center has a peak electrical load exceeding 10 megawatts or a daily water draw exceeding 100,000 gallons; Tier 2 storage has aggregate capacity between 81 and 600 kilowatt-hours or more than one storage technology in a room or enclosed area; Tier 3 exceeds 600 kilowatt-hours) and a statement that the ordinance remains in effect for ten years unless amended or repealed by voter approval of a ballot question. (Reconstructed from city notices 652 and 688 and news coverage; the certified question text was not retrieved.)
notes: Polls close 7 pm Central. Results page URL unverified. Butler County District Court ruled in August that the ordinance is legislative and may proceed by initiative (city notice 683).

title: Ban on data centers over 25 MW
target_project: Lightfield Energy Proximity Park (~300 acres, contract since terminated)
opponents: City of Ottawa (outside counsel called the ordinance administrative)
summary: Citizen-initiated ordinance prohibiting data centers that use more than 25 MW within city limits. Judge Eric Godderz ordered the question onto the ballot; a hearing on Oct 20, 2026 will decide whether the ordinance is legislative or administrative, which determines whether a YES vote takes effect. The city has since terminated the Lightfield sales contract.
ballot_text: Citizen-initiated ordinance barring the city from allowing or constructing any data center using more than 25 megawatts of power within city limits. Per KSHB and KOFO: a YES vote would restrict any data center built in Ottawa to no more than 25 megawatts; a NO vote would allow construction of data centers that use more than 25 megawatts. (Paraphrase; the certified question text was not retrieved.)
notes: Polls close 7 pm Central. Court hearing Oct 20, 2026.

target_project: Pending council data-center regulations (hearings Oct 16 and Nov 16)

summary: Non-binding question placed by township electors. The township is coterminous with the City of Bloomington. Council already passed a six-month moratorium (expires Nov 26) and is drafting rules limiting large data centers to the M2 district.
ballot_text: Should the City of Bloomington implement a moratorium on the creation of any large-scale data centers?
notes: Results come from the Bloomington Election Commission, not the McLean County Clerk. Polls close 7 pm Central. Wording confirmed by 25News (Oct 14, 2026); the official question page and specimen ballot are on the commission's site.

ballot_text: Should the Joliet City Council approve construction of AI data centers? (Yes - For the Measure / No - Against the Measure)

notes: A YES vote favors data centers. Who placed the question is unverified.

title: Advisory: restrictions on data centers countywide

proponents: Accountability for Data Center Development; Indivisible Jacksonville (1,100+ signatures)

(Wording per WLDS's October report; the petition-stage draft read: Should there be restrictions imposed on the construction of data centers in Morgan County? The certified ballot was not retrieved.)

Results post on the GBS portal (results.gbsvote.com). Polls close 7 pm Central.

title: Voter approval required for projects over $450M at the GM/JATCO site
target_project: Viridian Partners' proposed 800 MW, ~$8B data center campus on the former GM site (letter of intent lapsed)
summary: Direct legislation under Wis. Stat. 9.20 requiring that development agreements, projects, sales and leases at the city-owned GM/JATCO sites (1000 General Motors Dr. and 544 Kellogg Ave. plus adjacent parcels in the same development) involving more than $450 million in project costs be approved by a majority of Janesville electors; phased projects aggregate toward the threshold. The question does not mention data centers but was written to stop the Viridian campus; the city also has a separate data center moratorium.
ballot_text: Should approval of development agreements, development projects, sales, and leases at the GM/JATCO sites for projects over $450 million be decided by a majority vote of the electors? (Reconstructed from verbatim fragments reported by WMTV, the Gazette and the Badger Institute; the full sentence as printed was not retrieved. The ordinance covers 1000 General Motors Drive and 544 Kellogg Ave. plus adjacent properties in the same development, treats phased developments as one project, and does not use the words data center.)
notes: Polls close 8 pm Central. Janesville absentee ballots are counted centrally and reported separately.

title: Voter-locked ban on data centers in all zones
target_project: Pre-emptive; follows neighboring Monterey Park
summary: Affirms the council's existing zoning ban on data centers by voter action, so a future council cannot repeal it without going back to voters. Simple majority.
ballot_text: Data Centers Prohibited. Shall an ordinance be adopted affirming the Council adopted ban on "Data Centers" by amending the Alhambra Municipal Code to again define "Data Centers" and prohibit them in all zones of the City?
notes: Polls close 8 pm Pacific. LA County JSON feed: results.lavote.gov/electionresults/json?electionid=ID (June 2, 2026 primary was 4338; the Nov 3 id appears when the election is listed).

title: Allow data centers in the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area
target_project: Roughly 14,000 acres of city-owned desert outside the tortoise habitat easement
summary: City Charter section 144(1) requires voter approval of any new permitted use in the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area. A YES vote makes data centers an approved land use on the roughly 14,000 acres outside the habitat conservation easement; individual leases would still need the Land Management Plan process and council approval.
ballot_text: Should data center facilities be an approved land use within the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area outside of the Multi-species Habitat Conservation Easement? City explanation: if passed, the City Council would only be authorized to potentially enter into leases allowing data center facilities; any proposed project would still require further city review. If it fails, no data center facilities would be approved within the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area outside of the Multi-species Habitat Conservation Easement.
notes: A YES vote is the pro-data-center side. Polls close 7 pm Pacific. Wording per the city Explanation and Digest and Nevada Current. The 2024 NV SOS Clark County page listed Boulder City questions, so the SOS page should carry this one too.

title: Prohibit New Data Centers charter amendment
target_project: Pre-emptive (no project pending)
summary: Charter amendment prohibiting the permitting, construction, expansion or operation of new data centers within city limits, covering cloud, AI, crypto-mining and colocation facilities. Council enacted an ordinance ban in September to prevent an approval before the vote; proponents argue a charter provision is more durable because a future council could repeal an ordinance.
ballot_text: Charter amendment that would "prohibit the approval, construction, expansion, or operation of new data centers within the city" (phrase quoted from the ordinance at first reading, per ClickOrlando) and bar the city from issuing development approvals or permits for such facilities. The official ballot title and summary have not been retrieved; the "Charter Amendment 4" label comes from local coverage rather than an official source.
notes: Polls close 7 pm Eastern (Volusia is in the Eastern zone). The amendment is one of seven charter questions the council sent to the ballot Aug 3, 2026. Confirm the official number and summary on the Volusia County sample ballot.

title: Prohibit data centers citywide (General Plan amendment)
target_project: Proposed ~250,000 sq ft, up-to-50 MW data center on a former mall site
summary: Amends the General Plan land-use element to prohibit data centers citywide; changeable only by a future public vote. Widely described as the first voter-approved permanent data center ban in the country.
ballot_text: Community Act Prohibiting Data Centers. Shall the ordinance amending the City of Monterey Park General Plan to prohibit data centers citywide to protect air quality, drinking water resources and public health... (opening of the question per Resolution No. 2026-R6; the remainder, which references electricity and water rates and keeps the prohibition in place until voters end it, was not captured verbatim)
result_note: Passed 88.3% yes (10,321 to 1,362), certified LA County results as reported by secondary sources.
notes: Placement (citizen vs council) unconfirmed.

target_project: Vantage Data Centers / OpenAI-Oracle Stargate campus and the $458M TID No. 5
opponents: Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce and others (lawsuit pending)
summary: Bars the city from creating or approving a tax incremental district with a projected base value of $10 million or more, or project costs over $10 million, without voter approval. Prospective only; does not affect the Vantage campus already under construction.
ballot_text: Shall the City of Port Washington adopt the proposed ordinance, which, if adopted, would bar the City from creating or approving a Tax Incremental District that requires a large capital expenditure, or with a base value projected to or exceeding $10,000,000.00, or project costs exceeding $10,000,000.00 [...] (remainder, per coverage: unless approved by city electors at a referendum; verbatim excerpt per WTMJ's voter guide, cut off in the source)
result_note: Passed 66.4% yes (2,710 to 1,371), unofficial Ozaukee County count.
notes: Called the nation's first anti-data-center referendum. Lawsuit pending.

ballot_text: Advisory question, beginning with Should, asking whether the Village should authorize, support, participate in or facilitate municipal utility infrastructure and related improvements tied to a large-scale data center development within or affecting the Village. title: Bond and noise guarantee for hyperscale data centers seeking tax breaks
target_project: Province Group proposal (village declined its abatement/PILOT request in July)
summary: Citizen-initiated ordinance requiring any hyperscale data center developer (over 10,000 sq ft, over 5,000 servers, or over 50 MW) that seeks a tax abatement, PILOT or other special tax designation to first deposit a bond or escrow equal to at least the projected tax revenue over the project's 31-year life plus projected salaries for 200 full-time employees, with annual make-whole payments if projections fall short and assessments for environmental, standard-of-living or property-value effects. Also requires a noise guarantee of 50 dB by day and 45 dB overnight with council-set fines. Conditions the deal rather than banning the building.
ballot_text: Proposed ordinance requiring developers of hyperscale data centers that seek tax abatements or special tax designations to post a 31-year financial guarantee and meet noise limits (summary per Hoodline and the News-Herald; certified text not yet retrieved).
notes: Found Oct 15 as the jurisdiction missing from the earlier list; with Piqua (moved to Feb 2027) it reconciles Ballotpedia's 21 measures / 18 jurisdictions.
